The principles of design are `the foundational rules and guidelines artists and designers use to arrange the visual elements (such as line, color, shape, and texture) in a composition`.[[1]](https://www.vistaprint.com/hub/principles-of-design)[[2]](https://www.superside.com/blog/principles-of-design-guide)

### Core Principles of Design

- **Balance:** The distribution of visual weight in a layout. It can be *symmetrical* (mirrored on both sides), *asymmetrical* (different elements that still feel weighted equally), or *radial* (arranged around a central point).[[1]](https://guides.lib.berkeley.edu/design)[[2]](https://www.toptal.com/designers/ui/principles-of-design)
- **Contrast:** The use of opposing elements—such as dark vs. light, large vs. small, or bold vs. thin—to make specific parts of a design stand out and improve legibility.[[1]](https://www.toptal.com/designers/ui/principles-of-design)[[2]](https://www.superside.com/blog/principles-of-design-guide)
- **Emphasis:** Creating a focal point that draws the viewer's eye first. This highlights the most important message or call-to-action.[[1]](https://www.skillshare.com/en/blog/principles-of-design-you-need-to-master/)[[2]](https://www.vistaprint.com/hub/principles-of-design)[[3]](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/RZhMDlFm7Fg?vl=en)
- **Hierarchy:** The arrangement of elements to show order of importance, typically managed through scale, weight, and positioning (such as a main title versus body text).[[1]](https://www.adobe.com/express/learn/blog/8-basic-design-principles-to-help-you-create-better-graphics)[[2]](https://www.toptal.com/designers/ui/principles-of-design)
- **Repetition & Pattern:** Reusing the same colors, shapes, fonts, or motifs throughout a piece to build consistency, brand recognition, and rhythm.[[1]](https://www.superside.com/blog/principles-of-design-guide)[[2]](https://www.toptal.com/designers/ui/principles-of-design)[[3]](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/0FI93IolQK0)
- **Proportion & Scale:** The size relationship of different elements to one another, signaling what is dominant or subordinate.[[1]](https://www.toptal.com/designers/ui/principles-of-design)[[2]](https://www.skillshare.com/en/blog/principles-of-design-you-need-to-master/)
- **Movement:** The visual path or flow the viewer's eye takes as it travels across the composition.[[1]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UmHMVU6dceA&t=5)[[2]](https://guides.lib.berkeley.edu/design)[[3]](https://www.facebook.com/implantaire/videos/the-principles-of-designemphasis-balance-contrast-repetition-proportion-movement/910830120635094/)
- **White Space (Negative Space):** The empty or open area around and between elements. It prevents clutter and gives the design "breathing room".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design_principles)[[2]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UmHMVU6dceA&t=5)[[3]](https://www.facebook.com/implantaire/videos/the-principles-of-designemphasis-balance-contrast-repetition-proportion-movement/910830120635094/)
- **Unity & Harmony:** How all individual elements work together as a cohesive, complete whole rather than a random collection of parts.[[1]](https://www.figma.com/resource-library/graphic-design-principles/)[[2]](https://www.skillshare.com/en/blog/principles-of-design-you-need-to-master/)

You can explore detailed visual breakdowns and guides on how these rules apply to real-world projects via the [VistaPrint US Design Guide](https://www.vistaprint.com/hub/principles-of-design) or the [UC Berkeley Design Fundamentals Library](https://guides.lib.berkeley.edu/design).[[1]](https://www.vistaprint.com/hub/principles-of-design)[[2]](https://guides.lib.berkeley.edu/design)Are you working on a specific project—like a **logo, website, or poster** —and want to know which principle to apply next?
